lesson.title: Custer's Last Stand at the Little Bighorn
lesson.summary: On June 25, 1876, an alliance of Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors destroyed much of the U.S. 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer, the most famous Native victory of the Plains wars, though it ultimately accelerated rather than prevented the government's conquest of Lakota land.
lesson.body:
The battle's immediate cause, building on the previous chapter's account of broken treaties and railroad driven expansion, was gold. In 1874 an army expedition led by Custer himself explored the Black Hills of Dakota Territory and confirmed rumors of gold there, and prospectors poured onto the land soon afterward, violating the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty, which had guaranteed the Black Hills to the Lakota as part of the Great Sioux Reservation. When negotiations to purchase the Black Hills failed, the U.S. government declared that any Lakota, Cheyenne, or Arapaho people who had not reported to reservation agencies by early 1876 would be treated as hostile, effectively manufacturing a pretext for war against bands, including those led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse, who had never agreed to give up their land or their way of life.

On June 25 and 26, 1876, along the Little Bighorn River in Montana Territory, Custer led roughly 600 men of the 7th Cavalry against what turned out to be one of the largest Native encampments ever assembled on the Plains, a combined village of Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho that may have held several thousand people, including well over a thousand warriors. Custer badly underestimated the size of the village, divided his regiment into separate battalions under himself, Major Marcus Reno, and Captain Frederick Benteen, and attacked without adequate reconnaissance. Warriors led by Crazy Horse, Gall, and other leaders, while Sitting Bull served as spiritual leader after a recent Sun Dance vision that many believed foretold victory, surrounded and overwhelmed Custer's own battalion. Custer and roughly 210 men under his direct command were killed to the last man, and total 7th Cavalry deaths across the two day engagement reached about 268.

News of the defeat reached the eastern United States within days of the nation's Centennial Fourth of July celebrations in 1876, producing shock and outrage that hardened, rather than softened, American resolve. Within a year the Army had forced most Lakota bands onto reservations. Crazy Horse surrendered in 1877 and was killed in custody later that same year, while Sitting Bull led a small band into Canada before eventually returning and surrendering in 1881. In 1877, Congress unilaterally seized the Black Hills outright, ignoring the 1868 treaty's own requirement that any cession of Lakota land be approved by three quarters of adult Lakota men, a seizure the Lakota Nation has never accepted. In 1980 the U.S. Supreme Court itself ruled the taking unconstitutional and ordered financial compensation, which the Lakota have refused to this day, insisting on the return of the land itself rather than a monetary settlement.
